title: GEOG 531
section: What can a sample tell us?
text:
What can a sample tell us?
From Description and Exploration to Inference

What is Statistical Inference?

Making conclusions about a population using information in a sample!

How long do residents in a city spend their time commuting?

Making estimates about a population parameter.

Does providing shade in an area reduce exposure to heat?

Hypothesis testing : testing research claims

Is what we observe due to what we claim?
Or is it due to random chance/ natural variability in sampling?




70-minute route. Slides 1–9: 15 min. Slides 10–20: 25 min. Slides 21–29: 23 min. Slides 30–32: 7 min. For 50 minutes, use one R simulation per student per activity, then demonstrate the bulk-simulation code, and assign the final challenges for home. The student worksheet and R script contain all code. Nothing needs printing. Have students change seat_number in the setup, then pause after each single-simulation block to add a dot to the whiteboard. All datasets are fictional teaching examples. The setup defines student_seed as 1000 + the assigned seat number. Different students therefore contribute different results, with occasional coincident statistics expected. The HTML companion opens offline. In Quarto revealjs, S opens speaker view. The offline HTML uses N to show notes.

title: GEOG 531
text:
A city has a question

How long do residents spend commuting?

We can measure everyone, or learn from a sample.
Inference uses data and a probability model to learn about an unknown quantity and quantify uncertainty.

2 min. Invite examples: household water access, average summer temperature, flood preparedness. Distinguish describing observed cases from making a statement about unobserved residents or a process. Inference also supports experimental comparisons, not only surveys.

title: GEOG 531
text:
A result needs a reference
Survey: our sample mean commute is 25 minutes. How precisely does it estimate the population mean?
Experiment: shaded plots average 4°C cooler. Could random assignment produce a difference this large if shade had no effect?

2 min. The first is estimation, the second is hypothesis testing. Ask for instinctive answers before introducing vocabulary. Do not label an estimate precise just because there are many resamples.

title: GEOG 531
text:
Two different sources of variability







Random sampling
Random assignment




Which people enter the survey?
Which plots receive shade?


A different sample can give a different mean.
A different allocation can give a different group difference.



Each analysis must mimic the source of randomness in its study.

2 min. Whiteboard: draw a population and a sample on the left; a fixed set of 20 plots split into treatment groups on the right. Random sampling supports generalization to the sampling population. Random assignment supports a causal comparison for experimental units under the design. Neither automatically gives both.

title: GEOG 531
text:
Activity 1 · The commute lottery
A toy city has six equally common commute times:
5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 minutes
Its population mean is 17.5 minutes.
Prediction: will everyone obtain a sample mean of 17.5?

1 min. Each student runs the one-sample R block in the lab. The model is an independent draw from a large population with these six equally likely values. Replacement is appropriate for this toy model. These are not the eight survey observations used later.

title: GEOG 531
text:
Five draws make one sample

set.seed(student_seed)
my_sample <- city |>
  rep_sample_n(size = 5, reps = 1, replace = TRUE)
my_sample
my_sample |>
  summarise(sample_mean = mean(minutes), .groups = "drop")

Inspect five observations. Add one mean to the whiteboard.

4 min. The lab begins by loading tidyverse and infer, defining city, and setting student_seed to 1000 + the assigned seat number. Assign distinct numbers 1 through class size. Everyone runs only the one-sample block before the bulk simulation. Whiteboard: axis from 5 to 30 minutes. Ask why some values can occur twice and why different students get different means. No printing or paper cards are needed.

title: GEOG 531
text:
The population stays the same
The people drawn change. Their mean changes.
That movement from sample to sample is sampling variability.
The distribution of means from repeated samples is a sampling distribution.
Its standard deviation is the standard error.

2 min. Whiteboard: add a vertical marker at 17.5. Sample size five does not guarantee symmetry or closeness in any one sample. The across-sample distribution should center near 17.5. Contrast variability of individual commute times with variability of sample means.

title: GEOG 531
text:
What would twenty draws change?


    2026-10-20T10:46:11.757962 image/svg+xml   Matplotlib v3.10.8, https://matplotlib.org/                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           



12,000 simulated samples per sample size from the same toy city.


1 min. Ask students to predict before revealing the chart if possible. Larger samples tend to give less variable means. Under independent sampling, SE of a mean is σ/√n. Increasing sample size from 5 to 20 approximately halves SE. This reduces random variability, not sampling bias.

title: GEOG 531
text:
The same lottery in R

library(tidyverse)
library(infer)
city <- tibble(minutes = seq(5, 30, by = 5))
set.seed(student_seed + 1)
sampling_5 <- city |>
  rep_sample_n(size = 5, reps = 2000, replace = TRUE) |>
  summarise(stat = mean(minutes), .groups = "drop")

Change size = 5 to size = 20 and compare the spread.

1 min. rep_sample_n is an infer function, not a moderndive function. Its output is grouped by replicate, allowing summarise to calculate one mean per sample. The full script plots both sample sizes. Do not spend lecture time installing packages. All slide R chunks are displayed, not executed, and the supplied HTML presentation opens without R.

title: GEOG 531
section: Activity 2 · Does shade cool a surface?
text:
Activity 2 · Does shade cool a surface?
A fictional experiment uses 20 separated, comparable plots.
Random assignment gives 10 plots shade cloth and 10 plots sun. Measure surface temperature after one hour.
Question: does shade change surface temperature?

2 min. Independence, standardized measurement, no spillover, and complete random assignment are assumptions of this teaching experiment. The plots are not paired. Say these are constructed results, not measurements from a real study. Avoid any suggestion that naturally shaded sites were merely compared observationally.

title: GEOG 531
text:
The observed difference



Shade: 10 plots
Sun: 10 plots




28, 30, 31, 32, 33
32, 34, 35, 36, 37


34, 35, 36, 38, 39
38, 39, 40, 42, 43


Mean = 33.6°C
Mean = 37.6°C



D = mean(shade) − mean(sun) = −4.0°C

2 min. Whiteboard: write D = shade minus sun, circle the minus sign, and keep this definition visible. A negative difference means cooler in shade. Let students calculate or check the means. Identical temperatures in separate rows represent different plots and remain separate observations.

title: GEOG 531
section: A null model gives us a comparison
text:
A null model gives us a comparison
Null hypothesis: shade has no effect on any plot.
Under this sharp null, each plot keeps its observed temperature regardless of its assignment.
Alternative: shade changes temperature for at least some plots.
We will use differences in group means to detect a change.

2 min. This is an exact randomization test under the sharp null of no individual treatment effect. A simple permutation test does not in general test only equality of means under arbitrary different distributions. At an introductory level emphasize no effect and exchangeable assignments. A mean-difference test can have low power for changes that cancel in the mean. We choose a two-sided statistic and alpha .05 before examining the simulation.

title: GEOG 531
GEOG 531
section: What does one dot mean here?
text:
What does one dot mean here?

one_shuffle |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in means",
            order = c("shade", "sun"))

Add one difference to the board.
One dot represents one possible assignment under the null.

3 min. Whiteboard: new D axis from −10 to +10°C, with shade minus sun written above it. Each student adds their own statistic. Ask where the dotplot should center, then draw zero and observed ±4. The lab also supplies three-shuffle code, so every student can add three further dots if time permits. Discuss the class plot before anyone runs 10,000 permutations. Use the same seed for reproducibility, not to obtain fresh results by repeatedly resetting it.

title: GEOG 531
section: A two-sided p-value counts both tails
text:
A two-sided p-value counts both tails


2 min. Exact benchmark p = 0.024822. Include ties at −4 and +4. This exact enumeration uses distinct plots, even when temperatures match. Do not count unique value splits as equally likely. Classroom dots are a rough Monte Carlo approximation and may give zero tail points. That is not proof that the actual p-value is zero.

title: GEOG 531
text:
What does the p-value say?
Assuming the null model and study assumptions hold, the p-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed statistic.
For this test, “as extreme” means D ≤ −4 or D ≥ +4.
A smaller p-value indicates greater incompatibility with the null model.

2 min. Ask students to complete “If shade has no effect …”. Explicitly correct “the probability the null is true”, “the probability this happened by chance”, and “the probability the result will replicate”. The probability concerns a statistic under a specified model, not the truth of a hypothesis. Randomization probability here comes from possible treatment allocations.

title: GEOG 531
GEOG 531
text:
The computer counts the tails

null_dist |>
  get_p_value(obs_stat = observed, direction = "both")

visualize(null_dist) +
  shade_p_value(obs_stat = observed, direction = "both")

10,000 shuffles improve simulation precision.
They do not increase the experiment’s sample size.

1 min. infer uses its two-sided convention, based on doubling a tail probability. The exact null distribution in this balanced experiment is symmetric, so this agrees with counting |D| ≥ 4 in the exhaustive distribution. Finite Monte Carlo estimates can differ slightly. The full student script reports both approaches. No exact R simulation output is hard-coded in the slides.

title: GEOG 531
text:
Evidence, magnitude, and decisions
Observed difference: shade plots average 4°C cooler.
Evidence: the randomization test assesses compatibility with no effect.
Decision rule: with α = 0.05 set in advance, reject when p ≤ 0.05.
Would 0.049 and 0.051 justify very different scientific stories?

2 min. This dataset yields an exact p below .05. Reject the no-effect null under the experimental assumptions. Do not say prove shade works everywhere. Do not interpret statistical significance as effect importance. Alpha is a long-run Type I error control under the null, not a posterior probability of error for this result. Spatially separated plots do not automatically guarantee no spatial dependence; they are assumed independent here.

title: GEOG 531
section: Activity 3 · How long is the commute?
text:
Activity 3 · How long is the commute?
A separate fictional survey takes a simple random sample of eight residents from a large city population.
10, 15, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 50 minutes
Sample mean = 25 minutes.
How much uncertainty surrounds that estimate?

2 min. This is a survey, not an experiment and not the known lottery population. We treat the population as large and observations as independent. The two 15s represent two people. Eight observations make inspecting one resample manageable but form a deliberately small, somewhat skewed sample. Treat its percentile interval as a teaching approximation. A larger survey is preferable for substantive inference.

title: GEOG 531
section: The population is out of reach
text:
The population is out of reach
We would like many new samples from the city.
We have only one sample.
The bootstrap uses that sample as an approximation to the population and resamples it to estimate sampling variability.

1 min. Whiteboard: unknown population as a cloud, one eight-person sample, multiple resamples. The bootstrap distribution is conditional on the observed sample; it approximates rather than equals the true sampling distribution. Resampling cannot recover omitted subpopulations or unseen extremes.

title: GEOG 531
text:
Everyone makes a bootstrap sample

set.seed(student_seed + 20)
one_bootstrap <- commute |>
  specify(response = minutes) |>
  generate(reps = 1, type = "bootstrap")
one_bootstrap
one_bootstrap |> calculate(stat = "mean")

Inspect eight draws. Add one mean to a new board axis.

5 min. The lab defines the separate eight-person survey. Ask students to compare original values with the eight generated values. Some respondent observations repeat and others may be absent, although a particular resample can by chance use every respondent once. The two original 15s already represent different people, so repeated values alone do not identify which respondent was redrawn. One resample still has eight observations. Add each mean to a separate minutes axis marked at 25. Discuss the empirical distribution before 10,000 resamples. The lab also supplies three-bootstrap code.

title: GEOG 531
text:
Why does replacement matter?
Without replacement, selecting all eight respondents returns the same eight observations every time.
Every mean would equal 25.
type = "bootstrap" samples with replacement, allowing the composition and mean to vary while keeping n = 8.

1 min. Ask students what would happen if R simply reordered the eight survey rows and then took their mean. Shuffling row order alone does not generate uncertainty in a single mean. Replacement creates new empirical samples, not new real observations.

title: GEOG 531
GEOG 531
text:
The middle 95% gives an interval


2 min. Illustration interval: 17.500 to 33.750 minutes. Draw vertical lines leaving 2.5% in each tail. The central 95% of bootstrap statistics yields a percentile interval for the population mean. This is not an interval containing 95% of individual commute times. With n=8 and skew, nominal 95% coverage need not be accurate.

title: GEOG 531
text:
What does “95% confidence” mean?
It describes the interval-making procedure.
Across repeated random samples, a well-calibrated 95% procedure produces intervals that contain the fixed population mean about 95% of the time.
Our computed interval either contains that mean or misses it. We do not know which.

2 min. The parameter is fixed in the frequentist interpretation; intervals vary. “We are 95% confident that the population mean is between L and U” is conventional language, justified by procedure coverage. Do not assign a 95% frequentist probability to the fixed parameter falling in this realized interval. Bootstrap coverage is approximate, especially for tiny or skewed samples.

title: GEOG 531
text:
Repeated intervals, one population mean


1 min. These are not 100 resamples from one sample. Each interval starts with a new independent sample from the same population. The visualization intentionally uses an exact normal-mean interval, not the small commute-sample percentile bootstrap. Coverage is a long-run property, not a promise of exactly 95 successes out of 100.

title: GEOG 531
section: What a confidence interval does not say
text:
What a confidence interval does not say
“95% of residents commute for a time inside this interval.”
“95% of future sample means must fall inside this interval.”
“There is a 95% frequentist probability that the fixed mean lies in this computed interval.”
Each statement misinterprets the interval.

2 min. Have pairs rewrite one statement. Correct target: uncertainty about the population mean, assessed through repeated-sampling performance of the interval procedure. A narrow interval can be confidently wrong if the sampling frame excludes many residents. Do not use a bootstrap of a convenience sample to imply population representativeness.

title: GEOG 531
text:
Two simulations, two questions









Shuffling
Bootstrapping




Question
Is the statistic unusual under a null model?
How variable is our estimate?


Action today
Reassign outcomes to groups
Draw rows with replacement


What stays fixed?
Values and group sizes
Original sample and resample size


Typical center
Null value: 0 here
Observed estimate: 25 here


Output today
p-value
Confidence interval




2 min. Ask students to explain why a null distribution cannot simply serve as a confidence interval distribution. These are introductory workflows, not universal statements that bootstrap can never be used for testing or randomization can never be inverted for intervals. The two centers have different units here because we used different case studies.

title: GEOG 531
section: A geographic conclusion needs a design
text:
A geographic conclusion needs a design
Random sampling supports inference to the sampling population.
Random assignment supports a causal comparison for experimental units.
Nearby sites, repeated observations, and clustered households may require different resampling units.
More resamples cannot repair a biased sample.

2 min. Whiteboard: three nearby houses inside one neighborhood. If neighborhood is the independent unit, resampling individual houses can understate uncertainty. Mention cluster or spatial block resampling as later methods, without teaching them today. Restrict shuffles to what the assignment design actually permitted, for example within blocks. Do not use the simple code unchanged for dependent spatial data.

title: GEOG 531
text:
Three-minute exit ticket

What does one dot represent in each of our three distributions?
Why does shuffling preserve each outcome once while bootstrapping allows repeated observations?
A p-value is 0.03. Write one valid interpretation.
What changes when we increase resamples from 1,000 to 10,000? What changes when we increase sample size?


3 min. Answers: sampling means from new five-person samples; randomization differences under no effect; bootstrap means from resamples of the observed eight-person sample. No replacement preserves fixed experimental outcomes and group sizes; bootstrap replacement allows new empirical samples of original size. Valid p interpretation is conditional on null and assumptions, for as-extreme-or-more statistics. Reps reduce Monte Carlo error; sample size can reduce statistical uncertainty. Have students exchange answers or submit before leaving.

title: GEOG 531
text:
After class
Read: IMS Chapters 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.
Practice: Lesson on foundation of inference
Use the worksheet: change sample size, resample count, and confidence level. Predict each result before running it.

title: Inference by hand and in R
text: All examples are fictional. = Each student runs one simulation and contributes one statistic to the whiteboard before running many simulations. Work through each section in order in a fresh R session. The accompanying .R script contains the same workflows. Everyone needs a different assigned seat number. Record your number and run each block from its set.seed(...) line to reproduce your results at home. Do not run the entire worksheet before the class discussions.

title: Inference by hand and in R
text:
1. Sampling variability
In class: first run the setup and replace seat_number <- 1 with your assigned number. Run only the my_sample block. Inspect its five observations and calculate one sample mean. Add that mean to the whiteboard. Predict the class pattern before running 2,000 samples.
Prediction: what happens to the spread of sample means if the sample size increases from 5 to 20?

# Foundations of inference — Quantitative Methods in Geography
# All data are fictional. Run from the top, in a clean R session.
# Install once if needed:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "infer"))
library(tidyverse)
library(infer)

# Your instructor assigns everyone a different seat number: 1, 2, 3, ...
# Replace 1 with YOUR assigned number. Record it to reproduce your work.
seat_number <- 1
student_seed <- 1000 + seat_number
# Re-running a block with the same seed repeats the same random results.
# More replicates in generate() produce multiple simulations in one run.

# 1. SAMPLING VARIABILITY: known toy city, independent draws
city <- tibble(minutes = seq(5, 30, by = 5))
mean(city$minutes) # known population mean = 17.5

[1] 17.5



One sample first

title: Inference by hand and in R
text:
4. Optional investigations
The exact randomization check counts all equally likely allocations. The coverage function starts with a new original sample each time, rather than repeatedly resampling only the observed eight people. Run the commented calls explicitly if desired.

# OPTIONAL: exact check of the shuffle (184,756 assignments).
# Run explicitly if desired. Distinct plot IDs matter even for equal values.
exact_randomization <- function() {
  choices <- combn(seq_len(nrow(temperature)), 10)
  first_sum <- colSums(matrix(temperature$temp_c[choices], nrow = 10))
  exact_stats <- (2 * first_sum - sum(temperature$temp_c)) / 10
  tibble(assignments = length(exact_stats),
         exact_p = mean(abs(exact_stats) >= abs(observed$stat) - 1e-10))
}
# exact_randomization()

# OPTIONAL: approximate bootstrap coverage across genuinely new samples.
# This function is defined, but not run automatically.
# Each repetition starts with a new sample from a known normal population.
bootstrap_coverage <- function(repetitions = 100, n = 30, reps = 500) {
  set.seed(535)
  intervals <- map_dfr(seq_len(repetitions), function(i) {
    new_sample <- tibble(minutes = rnorm(n, mean = 25, sd = 5))
    limits <- new_sample |>
      specify(response = minutes) |>
      generate(reps = reps, type = "bootstrap") |>
      calculate(stat = "mean") |>
      get_confidence_interval(level = 0.95, type = "percentile")
    mutate(limits, sample_number = i, covers = lower_ci <= 25 & upper_ci >= 25)
  })
  print(summarise(intervals, coverage_fraction = mean(covers)))
  ggplot(intervals, aes(y = sample_number, color = covers)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = lower_ci, xend = upper_ci, yend = sample_number)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 25, linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(x = "Interval for the population mean", y = "New sample") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
}
# bootstrap_coverage()

text:
2.3 Q2. Predict before testing [7 points]
Using the maps, predict one broad spatial variation in event intensity and one local proximity pattern. Give a plausible geographic explanation for each. State a testable prediction for the difference between years and one reason that a difference could reflect event-type composition or reporting rather than a change in physical hazard. [4]
Define first- and second-order structure in your own words. Explain how independent events could still appear concentrated in one part of the state. [3]
Your response:






NoteA guide to careful interpretation



First-order structure concerns how expected event intensity or expected areal values vary across space, potentially with rainfall, elevation, land cover, exposure, or reporting opportunity. Second-order structure concerns dependence between locations after accounting for those expectations. Uniform independent points represent a restrictive null model.
Quadrat counts summarize spatial variation in counts; nearest neighbors summarize local spacing. Neither a rejection of uniformity nor short neighbor distances alone separates first-order variation from second-order dependence. Join counts, Moran’s I, and LISA describe neighbor association in areal values, but spatial trends and shared covariates can produce that association. A statistic does not uniquely identify the mechanism.

title: Homework 2: Is There a Pattern in the Storm?
text:
3.1 Worked example: quadrat analysis for 2015
The null is spatially uniform, independent event locations within South Carolina, conditional on the observed number of reports. We use the SC polygon, not its bounding rectangle, as the observation window. Edge quadrats contain different areas within SC; their expected counts must differ accordingly. A 4 × 4 grid is clipped to this window by spatstat.

Q15 <- quadratcount(X15, nx = 4, ny = 4)
plot(X15, main = "2015 reports and clipped quadrats", pch = 16, cex = 0.35)
plot(Q15, add = TRUE, col = "blue")

set.seed(53101)
qt15 <- quadrat.test(X15, nx = 4, ny = 4,
                     method = "MonteCarlo", conditional = TRUE,
                     alternative = "two.sided", nsim = 999)
qt15
plot(qt15, main = "2015: observed, expected, and Pearson residuals")

The Monte Carlo approach accommodates small expected counts in clipped coastal/border cells. A large Pearson statistic indicates more uneven counts than expected; an unusually small statistic indicates more even counts. The two-sided p-value alone does not tell you which. The simple variance-to-mean benchmark of 1 assumes equal-area quadrats; do not apply it uncritically to this clipped grid.

title: Homework 2: Is There a Pattern in the Storm?
text:
3.3 Worked example: nearest-neighbor analysis for 2015
The Clark–Evans ratio compares observed mean nearest-neighbor distance to the infinite-plane homogeneous Poisson benchmark, approximately \(1/(2\sqrt{\lambda})\), where \(\lambda=n/A\). Values below 1 suggest shorter spacing; values above 1 suggest more regular spacing. The finite observation window affects this benchmark.
We therefore use a Monte Carlo test in the actual SC window, with the same number of points and the same uncorrected statistic for observations and simulations. This calibrates the p-value for the window geometry. The uncorrected ratio itself still has edge effects; do not use an uncorrected asymptotic normal test.

nna_summary <- function(X) {
  lambda <- npoints(X) / area.owin(Window(X))
  observed <- mean(nndist(X))
  expected <- 1 / (2 * sqrt(lambda))
  tibble(n = npoints(X), mean_NN_m = observed,
         theoretical_CSR_NN_m = expected, R_uncorrected = observed / expected,
         fraction_zero_NN = mean(nndist(X) == 0))
}
nna_summary(X15)
set.seed(53102)
nn15 <- clarkevans.test(X15, correction = "none", method = "MonteCarlo",
                        alternative = "two.sided", nsim = 999)
nn15

section: 4.2 Worked example: random labeling of damage
text:
4.2 Worked example: random labeling of damage
Keep locations fixed, including their existing clustering. Let \(T\) be the mean absolute difference in log1p(damage) between each report and its nearest neighbor. Smaller \(T\) means greater similarity. log1p(x)=log(1+x) retains zeros and limits domination by very large marks. Shuffle the damage labels 999 times across these fixed locations. This tests random labeling, not CSR; its validity assumes labels are exchangeable under the null. Event type and geographic exposure may violate that assumption.

nn_damage_test <- function(M, nsim = 999, seed = 53103) {
  stopifnot(npoints(M) >= 3, all(is.finite(marks(M))), all(marks(M) >= 0))
  z <- log1p(marks(M))
  neighbor <- nnwhich(M) # With distance ties, one nearest neighbor is selected.
  Tstat <- function(v) mean(abs(v - v[neighbor]))
  observed <- Tstat(z)
  set.seed(seed)
  simulated <- replicate(nsim, Tstat(sample(z)))
  p <- (1 + sum(simulated <= observed)) / (nsim + 1)
  list(summary = tibble(n = length(z), observed_T = observed,
                       permutation_mean_T = mean(simulated),
                       p_similarity = p), simulated = simulated)
}
mark15 <- nn_damage_test(M15)
mark15$summary
hist(mark15$simulated, main = "2015: shuffled damage labels", xlab = "Mean NN log-damage difference")
abline(v = mark15$summary$observed_T, col = "red", lwd = 2)

Most points fall inside one county. A point exactly on a border can intersect more than one. We retain it once, assigning the lowest sorted GEOID as an explicit tie rule. assignment_audit <- tibble(row_id = storms_sc$row_id, matches = lengths(hits))
count(assignment_audit, matches)

assigned <- storms_sc |>
  mutate(county_GEOID = counties_sc$GEOID[county_index])

summaries <- assigned |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(county_GEOID, YEAR) |>
  summarise(n_events = n(),
            n_damage_known = sum(!is.na(PROP_DAMAGE_USD)),
            n_damage_missing = sum(is.na(PROP_DAMAGE_USD)),
            damage_known_sum = if (all(is.na(PROP_DAMAGE_USD))) NA_real_
                               else sum(PROP_DAMAGE_USD, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

  left_join(summaries, by = c("GEOID" = "county_GEOID", "YEAR")) |>
  mutate(no_reports = is.na(n_events),
         # No reports means zero recorded damage. Reports with ALL unknown
         # damage remain NA; partial totals are labeled as known-only sums.
         damage_known_sum = if_else(no_reports, 0, damage_known_sum),
         across(c(n_events, n_damage_known, n_damage_missing), ~replace_na(.x, 0L)))

  select(GEOID, NAME, ALAND) |>
  left_join(county_values, by = "GEOID") |>
  mutate(land_km2 = as.numeric(ALAND) / 1e6,
         events_per_1000_land_km2 = 1000 * n_events / land_km2) |>
  arrange(YEAR, GEOID)

6.1 Define the graph once and preserve county order
A queen neighbor shares a boundary or vertex; a rook neighbor shares a boundary segment. A neighbor graph defines what “nearby” means. Binary weights are appropriate for counting joins; row-standardized weights make a spatial lag the average of neighboring county values.

Our core variable is report density per 1,000 land km². Raw counts are also examined as a denominator sensitivity check. We retain numerical magnitudes instead of converting them into categories.

     xlab = "Standardized county report density", ylab = "Mean neighboring standardized density",
     main = "2015 Moran scatterplot")

The random-labeling null permutes numerical values among counties on the fixed graph. Its usual expected Moran’s I is \(-1/(n-1)\), rather than exactly zero. Positive autocorrelation means similar values tend to be adjacent; negative autocorrelation means dissimilar values tend to be adjacent. Positive I can reflect both high–high and low–low associations. It is not a map of where clusters occur and does not measure a first-order trend directly.

title: Homework 2: Is There a Pattern in the Storm?
text:
6.6 Worked example: local Moran’s I (LISA)
Local statistics locate county–neighbor associations. A positive local I can indicate high–high or low–low. A negative local I can indicate high–low or low–high. Classification requires the county’s standardized value and spatial lag as well as statistical evidence.
We use conditional permutations. For each county, its observed value is held fixed while other counties’ values supply shuffled neighbor values. These are different reference distributions from the global permutation test. Because 46 local tests create multiple-testing concerns, show both unadjusted and Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjusted results. BH is a useful exploratory false-discovery-rate procedure with assumptions about dependence; it does not guarantee that every highlighted county is a true finding.

make_lisa <- function(county_sf, listw, seed) {
  v <- county_sf$events_per_1000_land_km2
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(v)), sd(v) > 0)
  z <- as.numeric(scale(v))
  wz <- lag.listw(listw, z)
  local <- localmoran_perm(v, listw, nsim = 999, alternative = "two.sided",
                           iseed = seed, no_repeat_in_row = TRUE)
  # Select the two-sided permutation p-value, not the normal approximation
  # and not the folded [0, 0.5] pseudo-p column.
  print(colnames(local))
  p_column <- "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"
  if (!p_column %in% colnames(local)) {
    stop("Inspect localmoran_perm column names; identify its two-sided simulation p-value.")
  }
  p <- local[, p_column]
  quadrant <- case_when(
    z > 0 & wz > 0 ~ "High–High",
    z < 0 & wz < 0 ~ "Low–Low",
    z > 0 & wz < 0 ~ "High–Low",
    z < 0 & wz > 0 ~ "Low–High",
    TRUE ~ "At mean"
  )
  county_sf |>
    mutate(local_I = local[, "Ii"], z_value = z, lag_z = wz,
           quadrant = quadrant, p_local = p, p_BH = p.adjust(p, method = "BH"),
           lisa_raw = if_else(p_local < 0.05, quadrant, "Not significant"),
           lisa_BH = if_else(p_BH < 0.05, quadrant, "Not significant"))
}
lisa15 <- make_lisa(c15, w_W, seed = 53107)
lisa_colors <- c("High–High" = "#b2182b", "Low–Low" = "#2166ac",
                 "High–Low" = "#ef8a62", "Low–High" = "#67a9cf",
                 "At mean" = "white", "Not significant" = "grey85")

lisa_long15 <- lisa15 |>
  pivot_longer(c(lisa_raw, lisa_BH), names_to = "adjustment", values_to = "LISA")
ggplot(lisa_long15) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = LISA), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~adjustment) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = lisa_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "2015 local association in county report density",
       subtitle = "Two-sided local tests; alpha = 0.05", fill = "Local pattern") +
  theme_void()

lisa15 |> st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(NAME, n_events, events_per_1000_land_km2, local_I,
         z_value, lag_z, p_local, p_BH, lisa_raw, lisa_BH) |>
  arrange(p_local)

If no counties survive adjustment, report that result. Do not raise alpha, change the variable, or switch the weights merely to obtain clusters. “Not significant” means insufficient evidence under this setup; it does not establish spatial randomness or safety.

9.3 A damage-based county variable
Repeat global Moran’s I for log1p(damage_known_sum) only after checking damage completeness. Use known-only sums transparently; do not compare a partly observed county with a fully observed county as if totals were equally complete. If you subset counties with missing totals, rebuild the neighbor graph and inspect islands. Interpret this as association in reported damage, which combines hazard, exposed assets, reporting, and missingness. Log transformation changes the question and influence of extremes; it does not make damage dollars into normally distributed observations.

title: Homework 2: Is There a Pattern in the Storm?
text:
9.4 County versus tract scale
Download a common-vintage SC tract geography with tigris::tracts(state = "SC", year = 2024, cb = FALSE, class = "sf"). Reuse the point-assignment checks and full polygon-year skeleton at the tract scale. Calculate and compare the zero-event proportion before deciding whether a tract-based LISA is useful. Explain why the number of tracts is not the number of independent weather systems, and why this changes the multiple-testing burden.

title: GEOG 531
text:
What would 20 draws change?


1 min. Ask students to predict before revealing the chart if possible. Larger samples tend to give less variable means. Under independent sampling, SE of a mean is σ/√n. Increasing sample size from 5 to 20 approximately halves SE. This reduces random variability, not sampling bias.

Two classes, one modeling workflow



Class 1

Lab 1, then a logistic introduction

Our goal: explain the comparison a model estimates.

Two 75-minute periods. Class 1 includes 40 minutes of linear-model concepts, a 25-minute lab and a 10-minute logistic bridge. Class 2 includes two 15-minute lab blocks. The students already know confounders, mediators and moderators. Connect to those ideas rather than reteaching DAGs. Use arrows/Space to advance, Esc for overview and S for speaker view. The original scrolling lecture remains available as 01_lecture_notes.html.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
One simulated urban heat study
400 households, with one respondent per household.



Outcome
What is measured?




Indoor temperature
Degrees Celsius


Respondent heat illness
Yes or no during a fixed window


Household heat illness episodes
A count over measured person-weeks



The same canopy contrast appears in all three models.

All observations are synthetic, and each household is treated as independent. No real people or places are represented. The outcomes were generated separately conditional on specified predictors. They are not an observed biological chain from temperature to illness to episodes. The count follow-up window varies, while the binary outcome uses one common fixed window. This distinction matters for denominators. The labs contain the data dictionary.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Class 1: the causal question
Does greater residential tree canopy reduce indoor heat?



Decision
Our target




Unit
One household


Exposure
Tree canopy around the home


Outcome
Indoor temperature, °C


Contrast
10 percentage points more canopy


Effect
Total effect, including shade




Class 1, minutes 0–5. Ask students to identify the unit, exposure, outcome, contrast and total-effect target before revealing the entries. A 10 percentage point contrast means 20% to 30%, for example. We want the pathways through shade to remain part of the effect. The fitted analysis will use associational wording unless the causal assumptions are justified.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Which path needs adjustment?



Working DAG for indoor temperature.


Discuss: Which variable blocks a backdoor path? What happens if we add shade?

Class 1, minutes 5–12 begins here. Give students 45 seconds to trace the path canopy ← deprivation → temperature. Higher deprivation is associated with lower canopy and higher indoor temperature in this simulation. Deprivation is a common cause. Shade is a mediator. Roof is an independent outcome predictor in this particular simulation. The direct canopy-to-temperature arrow represents pathways other than the measured shade index. DAGitty identifies deprivation as the minimal adjustment set under these arrows, but does not verify the arrows or choose functional forms.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: From the DAG to the formula
text:
From the DAG to the formula



Variable
Decision for the canopy total effect




Deprivation
Include to block the backdoor path


Shade
Exclude to keep the mediated pathway open


Cool roof
Optional outcome predictor for precision



indoor_temp_c ~ canopy10 + deprivation + cool_roof

The question determines the adjustment set. More predictors do not necessarily make a causal model better. A collider can open a noncausal path, and a mediator changes the target. A separate collider example is canopy → study participation ← heat illness: conditioning on participation can induce an association. The cool-roof decision is specific to the supplied DAG; in a real study it could have a different causal role. Do not choose adjustment variables with stepwise procedures, p-values or the largest R-squared.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: A linear model describes a mean
text:
A linear model describes a mean
The fitted line describes average temperature at a predictor value.

A slope describes the change in that mean.
A residual is observed temperature minus fitted temperature.
Least squares chooses coefficients to minimize squared residuals.

A particular household can lie above or below its predicted mean.

Class 1, minutes 12–22 begins here. Keep this intuitive: regression does not claim each household follows the line exactly. Squaring prevents positive and negative residuals from cancelling and gives larger residuals greater weight. A mean prediction and a prediction for one new household answer different questions. No derivation of ordinary least squares is needed.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: Continuous predictor: first settle the unit
text:
Continuous predictor: first settle the unit
canopy10 = canopy_pct / 10



Change
Units of canopy10




20% to 30% canopy
+1


20% to 40% canopy
+2



10 percentage points differs from a 10% relative increase.

Ask students to calculate a 10% relative increase from 20% canopy: it is 22%, a two-percentage-point change. Rescaling canopy makes a coefficient easier to discuss without changing the model’s fitted values. A slope of -0.57 per canopy10 is a slope of about -0.057 per one percentage point. Students should always state the contrast and units rather than saying simply “a one-unit increase.”

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Binary predictor: a group comparison
cool_roof: 0 = absent, 1 = present.



Roof group
Mean indoor temperature




0: absent
33.78°C


1: present
32.43°C


Difference, 1 minus 0
−1.36°C



A binary predictor can appear in a linear regression.

In a model with only the binary roof variable, the intercept is the mean of group 0 and the slope is the difference between group 1 and group 0. These values are from the supplied CSV. Ask which subtraction order matches the coefficient. The outcome family is chosen from the outcome, not from whether a predictor is binary. For a predictor with more than two categories, use a factor and state the reference category, rather than treating arbitrary category codes as equally spaced quantities.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
The adjusted model in R
m2 <- lm(
  indoor_temp_c ~ canopy10 + deprivation + cool_roof,
  data = d
)

coef_table(m2)
~ means “modeled using.” The predictors follow it.
The helper displays coefficients and 95% intervals.

Students receive this code in Lab 1. They do not need to memorize it. The source helper uses base-R covariance estimates and t intervals for linear models. Data loading and source(“R/helpers.R”) are already included in each lab. The lecture snippets are static examples so the slides render without running R. If data or specifications change, update the slides’ displayed numerical tables from the freshly fitted models.

The coefficient table

All coefficients use the outcome’s units: °C.

These estimates are from the same model as the lecture notes and labs. Read the canopy row first, because canopy is our exposure of interest. The other coefficients have conditional associational interpretations. Their presence in a canopy-adjusted model does not automatically identify a causal effect for every other predictor. A separate exposure requires its own causal question and adjustment reasoning.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Interpreting the canopy coefficient
At the same deprivation category and roof status,
10 percentage points more canopy is associated with
0.57°C lower mean indoor temperature.
For 20% versus 40% canopy, the fitted difference is about −1.14°C.

The 20-percentage-point contrast is two units of canopy10, so multiply -0.56753 by two. This assumes the linear model’s constant canopy slope is adequate across the contrast. Ask a student to supply the units and another to supply what is held constant. We say “associated with” here because fitting a regression does not establish the underlying causal assumptions.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: Interpreting a binary predictor and the baseline
text:
Interpreting a binary predictor and the baseline
Cool roof: roof = 1 homes have a fitted mean 1.37°C lower than roof = 0 homes, at the same canopy and deprivation.
Intercept: the fitted mean at canopy = 0%, deprivation = 0 and roof = 0.
Our observed canopy starts at 5%. This intercept extrapolates.

Contrast the unadjusted difference of -1.36 with the adjusted difference of -1.37. Similarity here reflects the simulation and does not eliminate the need for causal reasoning. An intercept can be essential to the model even when its zero-predictor scenario has little substantive support. Centering canopy at a meaningful value would change the intercept’s interpretation while leaving the canopy slope and fitted values unchanged.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
What does “holding constant” mean?
The model compares predictions at the same values of the other included variables.
An additive model assumes the same canopy slope for both roof groups.
A moderator changes a comparison across groups. We represent that with an interaction.

Regression does not physically hold anything constant. It also does not guarantee that all requested covariate combinations are supported by the data. The optional Lab 1 extension uses canopy10 * cool_roof. In that model, the canopy coefficient is the slope at roof = 0 and the interaction is the difference in slope for roof = 1. Connect the term “moderator” from their previous work to this model representation. Keep extended interaction practice outside the core class time.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Before adjusting: predict the direction
In this study:

Higher deprivation goes with less canopy.
Higher deprivation goes with higher temperature.

Discuss: Will the crude canopy slope look more or less strongly cooling than the deprivation-adjusted slope?

Class 1, minutes 22–30 begins here. Give pairs one minute to predict, using the open backdoor path. The expected answer is that the crude association is more negative: part of the deprivation contrast is incorrectly attributed to canopy in the crude comparison. Adjustment can move an estimate toward zero, away from zero, or reverse its sign. Do not teach “adjustment always shrinks an effect.”

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: Comparing everyone and comparing within groups
text:
Comparing everyone and comparing within groups



Crude and deprivation-adjusted canopy associations in simulated households.



The dashed line is the crude regression. The colored lines come from the model adjusted for deprivation only, comparing canopy within a deprivation category. The two colored groups occupy different parts of the canopy range. Pooling them makes the negative canopy association steeper. The lines extend across the displayed range to aid comparison; support is thinner near the extremes. Ask students to describe the contrast in words before showing the numerical table.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
What changed after adjustment?



Model
Canopy slope, °C per 10 percentage points




Crude
−1.053


Adjust for deprivation
−0.571


Also include cool roof
−0.568



The DAG explains why we adjust. A coefficient change alone does not establish confounding.

The initial difference follows the known backdoor pathway in the simulated study. Adding cool roof changes the canopy coefficient very little and narrows its interval. Roof helps explain some temperature variation while being independent of canopy by construction. Do not choose adjustment sets by a mechanical percent-change rule. In logistic models, non-collapsibility provides an additional reason that changed coefficients need not diagnose confounding.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: Adding a mediator changes the question
text:
Adding a mediator changes the question



Model
Canopy slope




Deprivation and roof adjusted
−0.568°C


Also adjust for shade
−0.213°C



Including shade blocks part of the pathway we wanted in the total effect.
A smaller coefficient does not show that the earlier model was wrong.

This optional comparison is useful even if students do not run the mediator model in class. The simulation’s true total effect is -0.60°C per 10 percentage points and its direct effect is -0.25°C. The sample estimates differ from these truths. In real data, a direct-effect interpretation requires additional causal assumptions, including careful consideration of mediator–outcome confounding. Adding a mediator does not automatically identify a direct causal effect.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
The estimate includes sampling uncertainty
Canopy coefficient: −0.57°C per 10 percentage points.
95% interval: approximately −0.67 to −0.47°C.

Report the estimate, interval, contrast and adjustment set.
A small p-value does not establish causation or practical importance.
The interval does not account for every uncertainty in the design.


Class 1, minutes 30–33. Explain that standard errors describe sampling variability. Under repeated sampling and the method’s assumptions, 95% intervals constructed this way cover the target parameter about 95% of the time. They do not incorporate all uncertainty about DAG arrows, selection, measurement, omitted causes or functional form. Distinguish a confidence interval for a mean from a prediction interval for one new household, which is usually wider. Keep inferential derivations outside the class.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Two kinds of model checks







The comparison
The fitted model




Is the adjustment set justified?
Is the conditional mean shape adequate?


Are comparable observations available?
Does the uncertainty calculation fit the data?


Could measurement or selection bias matter?
Do unusual observations dominate?



Residual plots help assess model behavior. They cannot prove causal identification.

Class 1, minutes 33–40 begins here. Separate identification assumptions from statistical assumptions. No amount of model fit can verify that all common causes have been measured. Overlap can be examined from predictor distributions, while exchangeability needs design and substantive reasoning. Independence also relies heavily on how observations were collected. Explain that a model can fit observed outcomes very well while answering the wrong causal question.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
What do these patterns suggest?



Four deliberately constructed residual patterns.



Ask students to name a concern and an action for each panel. A: no dominant visual pattern, which is reassuring but not proof. B: curvature suggests a mean-model problem, potentially requiring nonlinear terms or interactions. C: a widening spread raises concerns about ordinary homoskedastic SEs. D: runs in spatially ordered observations suggest dependence, requiring location/order and sampling information. These are illustrative patterns, separate from the lab data.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Which response fits the problem?



Concern
A useful next step




Curved residual pattern
Reconsider the mean model


Nonconstant error variance
Consider HC3 robust uncertainty


Spatial or grouped dependence
Examine location, time and grouping


Influential point
Check data and model sensitivity



Normality concerns the conditional errors for normal-theory inference. X and Y need not themselves be normal.

HC3 changes the estimated uncertainty but leaves OLS coefficients unchanged. It does not fix a wrong conditional mean, unmeasured confounding, selection or spatial dependence. A Q–Q plot helps assess residual tails; normal residuals are particularly relevant to exact small-sample inference, not to computing an OLS line. Also note that perfect multicollinearity prevents unique coefficient estimation, while strong imperfect collinearity can destabilize estimates and widen intervals. Do not remove unusual observations automatically.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Lab 1: a DAG-based linear model
25 minutes · Open 02_lab_linear.qmd.

Choose the adjustment set.
Compare crude and adjusted estimates.
Interpret continuous and binary predictors.
Inspect residuals and overlap.

One partner runs the code. The other explains. Switch after Q2.

Class 1, minutes 40–65. Use five pairs for the ten students. On Zoom, use breakout rooms with a shared response document. Ask pairs for one continuous-predictor interpretation, one binary-predictor interpretation and one diagnostic judgment when they return. The optional mediator, HC3, interaction and influence exercises are outside the 25-minute core. If a student has setup problems, pair them with a working partner rather than letting software trouble replace the conceptual exercise.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: The outcome can change while the predictors stay
text:
The outcome can change while the predictors stay
Now the outcome is respondent heat illness, coded 0 or 1.
A straight-line probability model can predict below 0 or above 1.
Logistic regression describes an S-shaped probability curve that stays between 0 and 1.
The outcome selects the family.

Class 1, minutes 65–75 begins here. Each household contributes one respondent observed over a common fixed binary-outcome window. The same canopy/deprivation/roof predictors can be used with a different outcome family. Linear probability models exist and can be useful, but this week introduces logistic regression. Emphasize the outcome-versus-predictor distinction again. The continuous predictor does not make the outcome continuous, and a binary predictor does not force a logistic model.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Three outcomes, three model scales








Outcome
Model and link
Mean on the response scale




Temperature, °C
Linear, identity
Mean temperature


Respondent illness, 0/1
Binomial, logit
Probability


Episode count
Poisson, log
Expected count



A GLM links the outcome’s mean to an additive predictor score.

This is an orientation slide. Students need not memorize the link formulas. The family describes the outcome’s conditional distribution, while the link connects the mean to the predictor score. Ordinary linear regression is also a Gaussian/identity special case within the wider GLM framework. An exposure offset will make the Poisson model’s slope coefficients rate comparisons in Class 2.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Our first logistic model
logit_model <- glm(
  heat_illness ~ canopy10 + deprivation + cool_roof,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = d
)
The canopy coefficient is about −0.340 in log-odds.
exp(-0.340) is about 0.712, an odds ratio.

Introduce the change from lm to glm and the explicit family argument. Do not work through odds arithmetic yet unless time permits. The exponentiated slope is an odds ratio; the exponentiated intercept is baseline odds, not a group contrast. Tell students they will return to this exact number and compute probabilities at the start of Class 2.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Class 1 exit questions

What chooses the family: the outcome or a predictor?
Which variable blocks the canopy backdoor path?
If an odds ratio is 0.70, can we say probability is 30% lower?

Bring a short explanation to the next class.

Expected answers: outcome; deprivation; no, an odds ratio multiplies odds, while the probability change depends on the baseline profile. Collect short answers or ask students to put them in the shared response document. This provides a retrieval prompt at the next meeting and lets you identify whether the outcome/predictor distinction is secure before introducing Poisson regression.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: Class 2: same design questions, new scales
text:
Class 2: same design questions, new scales
Today we will interpret odds ratios, calculate probabilities, and model episode rates.
For each GLM, deprivation remains a common cause of canopy and the outcome.
The shade mediator belongs to our separate temperature example.

Class 2, minutes 0–8. Retrieve the Class 1 exit answers without notes, then compare in pairs. The simplified outcome-specific GLM DAG is deprivation → canopy, deprivation → outcome, canopy → outcome and roof → outcome. Roof is independent of canopy by simulation design. Remind students that the outcomes were generated separately to keep the model-family teaching clear. Do not treat fitted temperature as a biological predictor in these separate GLM examples. A causal interpretation still requires the design, adjustment, support and model assumptions.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: Probability and odds use different denominators
text:
Probability and odds use different denominators



If probability is…
Odds are…




0.20
0.20 / 0.80 = 0.25


0.50
0.50 / 0.50 = 1.00


0.80
0.80 / 0.20 = 4.00



An odds ratio multiplies odds. Probability stays between 0 and 1.

Class 2, minutes 8–20 begins here. Probability compares events with all outcomes, whereas odds compare events with non-events. Use a group of 100 people if students need counts: 20 events and 80 non-events produces probability .20 and odds .25. An OR of .5 applied to baseline p=.5 produces odds .5 and probability one-third, not .25. No algebra beyond these comparisons is needed.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Interpreting logistic slopes



Predictor
Odds ratio
95% interval




Canopy, per 10 percentage points
0.712
0.573 to 0.883


Cool roof, 1 vs 0
0.393
0.233 to 0.663



At the same deprivation and roof status, 10 percentage points more canopy is associated with 28.8% lower odds of respondent illness.
The null odds ratio is 1.

For roof, hold canopy and deprivation fixed and compare roof = 1 with roof = 0: estimated odds are 60.7% lower. These are conditional association statements. The intervals are normal-approximation Wald intervals on the log-odds scale, exponentiated. Do not call the canopy effect a 28.8 percentage point decrease or a 28.8% decrease in probability. Also remind students that a changed OR after adjustment is not proof of confounding, because ORs are non-collapsible. Keep the technical term in notes unless students ask.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: Predicted probabilities give a familiar scale
text:
Predicted probabilities give a familiar scale
For deprivation = 0 and cool roof = 0:



Canopy
Predicted illness probability




20%
30.8%


40%
18.4%



Difference: −12.4 percentage points.
These are point predictions for two specified profiles.

The contrast spans 20 percentage points, or two units of canopy10. Its OR is 0.712 squared, about .506, which is a different quantity from the -12.4 percentage point probability difference. These are neither observed group proportions nor population-standardized marginal effects. They do not include uncertainty intervals for the predictions or their difference. A different baseline profile generally produces a different probability difference under the same log-odds slope.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Predicting in R
homes <- data.frame(
  canopy10 = c(2, 4),
  deprivation = 0, cool_roof = 0
)

predict(logit_model, newdata = homes,
        type = "response")
type = "response" returns probabilities for a logistic model.

Read each newdata row as a hypothetical household profile. canopy10=2 means 20% canopy. The fixed values make the adjustment comparison explicit. In Lab 2A, students attach the predictions as a new table column and calculate second minus first with diff(). Keep the row order unchanged when interpreting the sign. If students ask about a policy effect across everyone, explain that averaging over the population’s covariate profiles is a different, more advanced task.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: A constant OR can mean changing probability differences
text:
A constant OR can mean changing probability differences



Fitted illness probabilities at two deprivation categories, holding cool roof at 0.



This is the logistic half of the earlier side-by-side GLM figure, redrawn as its own slide. Both groups share a canopy slope on the log-odds scale in this additive model. Their probability differences need not match because the conversion to probability is nonlinear. This alone does not imply a canopy-by-deprivation interaction in log-odds. Lines are point predictions without uncertainty bands and extend across the displayed range; check support before choosing a substantive contrast.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Lab 2A: odds and probabilities
15 minutes · Open Part A of 03_lab_glm.qmd.

Confirm what 0 and 1 mean.
Interpret an OR and its interval.
Predict two illness probabilities.
Read the calibration table and convergence result.

Return with an odds statement and a probability statement.

Class 2, minutes 20–35. calibration_table groups predicted probabilities in .2-wide bins, then compares observed proportions with mean fitted probabilities and reports bin sizes. It is an in-sample screen, not validation on new data. The helper’s implementation is not a learning objective. Ask pairs to distinguish a mean fitted probability from an observed bin proportion. Convergence is reassuring but does not prove correct specification, no separation, no confounding or independence.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Counts depend on observation opportunity



Household
Episodes
Person-weeks
Episodes per 100 person-weeks




A
4
100
4


B
2
20

A has more episodes. B has the higher observed rate.
Person-weeks = people × weeks observed.

Class 2, minutes 35–48 begins here. Four people observed for ten weeks contribute 40 person-weeks. Our household count outcome allows repeated illness episodes, so it is not a count of distinct people with illness. Household size and count follow-up vary in the data. A raw count comparison mixes differences in rates with differences in exposure. The desired scientific target is an episode rate, so we supply an exposure offset.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: Poisson regression and an exposure offset
text:
Poisson regression and an exposure offset
Poisson regression models a nonnegative integer count.
Its log link makes expected counts positive.
offset(log(person_weeks))
The offset coefficient is fixed at 1. At the same predictor values, twice the exposure implies twice the expected count.

The offset supplies observation opportunity and imposes proportionality between exposure and expected count at a fixed covariate profile. This is a modeling assumption, not an automatic truth. It does not replace adjustment for measured common causes. Zero counts are valid; zero exposure is not valid for this log offset. A raw count model can be appropriate when exposure is equal or when the scientific target is an unstandardized count. Here the explicit target is a rate comparison.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
The count model in R
count_model <- glm(
  heat_episodes ~ canopy10 + deprivation + cool_roof +
    offset(log(person_weeks)),
  family = poisson(link = "log"), data = d
)

coef_table(count_model, exponentiate = TRUE)
Keep the count on the left. Supply exposure through the offset.

Do not place a precomputed noninteger rate on the left of an ordinary Poisson count likelihood. The observed count is the response and exposure belongs in the offset. This gives conditional rate comparisons when the exposure assumption is suitable. The helper exponentiates the slope coefficients and their Wald intervals. The exponentiated intercept is a baseline rate per person-week, not a rate ratio for a contrast.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Interpreting incidence rate ratios



Predictor
Rate ratio
95% interval




Canopy, per 10 percentage points
0.754
0.688 to 0.827


Cool roof, 1 vs 0
0.655
0.518 to 0.828



At the same deprivation and roof status, 10 percentage points more canopy is associated with a 24.6% lower episode rate.
The null rate ratio is 1.

For the binary roof predictor, compare roof = 1 with roof = 0 at the same canopy and deprivation: estimated rate is 34.5% lower. Avoid calling this an odds ratio, probability change, or temperature difference. IRR refers to episodes per unit exposure, and repeated events are allowed. Causal interpretations require appropriate identification assumptions just as with the linear and logistic models.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: Expected counts at a specified exposure
text:
Expected counts at a specified exposure
For deprivation = 0 and cool roof = 0:



Canopy
At 100 person-weeks
At 200 person-weeks




20%
2.78 episodes
5.56 episodes


40%
1.58 episodes
3.16 episodes



Counts double when exposure doubles. The predicted rates stay the same.
An expected count can be fractional.

The exact predictions are 2.77855 and 1.58101 at 100 person-weeks, doubling to 5.55710 and 3.16203 at 200. Use predict(…, type=“response”) and include person_weeks in newdata. The predicted rates remain .02779 and .01581 per person-week. Expected counts are averages across comparable settings, whereas each observed count is an integer. All predictions on this slide are points without prediction or confidence intervals.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Lab 2B: counts, rates and dispersion
15 minutes · Continue Part B of 03_lab_glm.qmd.

Identify the count and exposure.
Fit the Poisson model with an offset.
Interpret an IRR and predict counts.
Compare conditional dispersion in two outcomes.

Switch driver and interpreter roles.

Class 2, minutes 48–63. Keep the exposure explanation central. If pairs finish early, ask them to explain why modeling precomputed rates as Poisson counts is unsuitable. The optional quasi-Poisson extension is outside the core 15 minutes. In the dispersion exercise, episodes_extra is a separate outcome constructed with additional conditional variation, not a modification that students should apply to their real outcome data.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Logistic diagnostics ask different questions







Check
Why it matters




0/1 coding
The model predicts P(Y = 1)


Warnings or extreme coefficients
Possible separation or instability


Observed vs fitted probabilities
Possible mean-model mismatch


Continuous-predictor shape
Additivity is on the log-odds scale



Binary residuals do not need to look normally distributed.

Class 2, minutes 63–71 begins here. A calibration table is a useful simple screen, but an aggregate or in-sample match cannot establish the correct functional form or performance elsewhere. Sparse categories, large coefficients, huge SEs or convergence warnings should trigger inspection. Convergence itself does not rule out a practically problematic fit. The identification, measurement, support, influence and independence concerns from linear regression still apply to GLMs. The raw outcome is binary by construction, so a normality test is irrelevant to choosing the logistic family.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Poisson variation is conditional
The Poisson model sets variance equal to the mean given the predictors and exposure.



Outcome
Pearson dispersion ratio




Main episode count
0.97


Deliberately more variable count
1.79



A value well above 1 prompts investigation of extra conditional variation.

The ratio is the sum of squared Pearson residuals divided by residual degrees of freedom. It is a rough screen, not a hard cutoff or formal pass/fail test, particularly with sparse counts. Raw marginal count variance exceeding raw mean is not sufficient because predictors and exposure differ. Investigate mean form, missing predictors, reporting, influence and dependence. Quasi-Poisson or negative binomial can address some extra conditional variance, but neither automatically fixes unmeasured confounding or spatial dependence. Normal count residuals are not required.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: The same contrast on three scales
text:
The same contrast on three scales
For 10 percentage points more canopy, at the stated other predictor values:

The family changes the scale. The causal question still needs a justified design.

Ask students to explain each row without using the word “effect” unless they state the causal assumptions. Make clear that the rows concern three different simulated outcomes, not three estimates of one identical outcome effect. A continuous or binary predictor can appear in all three families. Adjustment choices still come from the exposure/outcome-specific causal diagram, while link and outcome-family assumptions govern interpretation and model adequacy.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
section: Exit ticket and the next modeling question
text:
Exit ticket and the next modeling question

Choose a family for temperature, any respondent illness and episode count.
Explain the difference between −0.57°C, OR = 0.71 and IRR = 0.75.
What if residuals cluster among neighbors, or households repeat within neighborhoods?

Next week: spatial dependence and hierarchical structure.

Class 2, minutes 71–75. Collect a three-sentence exit ticket. Expected families are linear, binomial-logit and Poisson-log with a person-week offset for the rate question. Neighborhood clustering and repeated observations challenge independence and ordinary uncertainty calculations. Obtain geographic coordinates or neighborhood IDs, time/order and sampling details before choosing a structure. Spatial proximity and hierarchical grouping are distinct: a random intercept alone need not remove all residual spatial dependence. End the core presentation here; the following slides are optional references.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Optional reference: moderators and interactions
lm(indoor_temp_c ~ canopy10 * cool_roof + deprivation,
   data = d)



Quantity
Interpretation




canopy10
Canopy slope for roof = 0


canopy10:cool_roof
Difference in canopy slope for roof = 1


Sum of the two
Canopy slope for roof = 1




Appendix, outside the timed core. The simulation contains no true canopy-by-roof interaction. A fitted nonzero interaction can still arise from sampling variation. Compare the interaction estimate and uncertainty directly. One group’s slope having p<.05 and the other not having p<.05 does not itself establish that the slopes differ. Interaction is scale-specific: differences in probability contrasts do not automatically imply interaction in an additive log-odds model.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Optional reference: robust uncertainty
coef_table(m2)
coef_table(m2, robust = TRUE)  # HC3
The fitted OLS coefficients stay the same. Standard errors and intervals can change.
HC3 addresses heteroskedastic inference under suitable independence assumptions. It does not repair the causal design or the mean model.

Appendix. In this dataset the ordinary canopy SE is .05109 and HC3 SE is .05092, a small difference consistent with the roughly homoskedastic simulation. Cluster-robust covariance estimation addresses a different dependence structure and needs appropriate cluster information and sufficient clusters. Leave implementation of clustered/spatial methods for next week. The supplied hc3_vcov function is base R; students need not memorize its algebra.

title: From causal diagrams to regression
text:
Optional reference: outcome-family checks







Model
Outcome and main statistical checks




Linear
Conditional mean form, variance, influence, residual tails


Logistic
Binary coding, log-odds mean form, separation, calibration


Poisson
Integer count, log-mean form, positive exposure, dispersion



For all: adjustment, overlap, measurement, selection and independence.

Appendix. No diagnostic can prove all assumptions. Sampling weights may also matter when inclusion probabilities vary, and measurement error or imperfect proxies can undermine causal adjustment. Perfect collinearity prevents identification of separate coefficients; strong imperfect collinearity can produce instability. Highlight issues relevant to students’ projects rather than turning the week into a checklist of statistical tests.
